(p-264) Surat al-Fajr (The Dawn)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿By the dawn﴾. This is an oath by which God the Exalted swore. Al-fajr is the breaking of morning light from the horizon of the east. There are two dawns. The first of them is elongated like the tail of a wolf (dhanab al-sirhan), appearing as a column of light with no width, then it disappears into a darkness that intervenes. This dawn is called al-fajr al-mubashshir (the heralding dawn) for the morning. Some call it al-kadhib (the false dawn), because it has been "denied" the morning.

It is part of the night and has no effect on prayer or fasting.

As for the second, it is elongated in its light and spreads across the horizon, and it is called al-fajr al-sadiq (the true dawn), because it tells you the truth about the morning. The poet said:

*It drove away the attacking dogs, and increased their fire with the dhu al-subh al-musaddiq, which flutters.*

On it depends the ruling of prayer and fasting, and we have mentioned that earlier.

Regarding God's oath by the dawn there are four sayings. The first: He meant by it the day, and expressed it as "dawn" because it is its beginning. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: al-fajr is the morning that begins the day each day. This was said by Ali, may God be pleased with him.

The third: He meant by it the dawn prayer. This is also related from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: He meant by it the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) specifically. This was said by Mujahid.

Regarding ﴿and ten nights﴾, which is a second oath, there are four sayings. The first: they are the ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah. This was said by Ibn Abbas, and Abu al-Zubayr related from Jabir that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "(By the dawn and ten nights.) He said: The ten of al-Adha."

The second: they are ten from the beginning of Muharram. This was reported by al-Tabari.

The third: they are the last ten nights of Ramadan. This is related from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: they are the ten of Musa, peace be upon him, which God the Exalted completed for him. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: they are the sunset prayer (maghrib), its even part being two rak'as and its odd part the third rak'a. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Abu al-Aliya.

The third: the even is the Day of Sacrifice, and the odd is the Day of Arafah. This was narrated by Ibn al-Zubayr from Jabir from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The fourth: the even is the two days of Mina, the eleventh and twelfth of Dhu al-Hijjah, and the odd is the third day by counting them. This was said by Ibn al-Zubayr.

The fifth: the even is the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah, and the odd is the three days of Mina. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The sixth: the even is creation of every thing, and the odd is Adam and Hawwa. This is because Adam was single, so he was made even by his wife Hawwa, becoming even after being odd. This was narrated by Ibn Nujayh.

The ninth: it is the number, because all of it is even and odd. This was said by al-Hasan.

It is also possible (an eleventh): the even is that which grows, and the odd is that which does not grow.

﴿And the night when it passes﴾. This is a fourth oath, and regarding it there are three aspects.

The first: it is the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr), because mercy spreads in it and it is singled out for increased reward.

The second: it is specifically the night of Muzdalifah, because people gather in it for obedience to God. Muhammad ibn Ka'b was asked about God's saying ﴿and the night when it passes﴾, and he said: "Travel by night, O traveler, and do not spend the night except at Jam'," meaning Muzdalifah.

The third: He meant the generality of the whole night.

The first: when it grows dark. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: when it moves on, because the night moves with the movement of the sun and the celestial sphere, so it shifts from horizon to horizon. From this is the saying of people: "The night came and the day departed."

The third: when its people travel through it, because al-sara is travel by night.

﴿Is there in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾ Regarding "dhu hijr" there are five sayings among the commentators. The first: for one who has intellect (dhu 'aql). This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: for one who has forbearance (dhu hilm). This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: for one who has religion (dhu din). This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The fourth: for one who has a veil/restraint (dhu sitr). This was said by Abu Malik.

The third: Alexandria. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The ninth: that God the Exalted crushed them with a crushing, making them decayed (rameem), and for this reason He named them. This was said by al-Suddi.

One: meaning they cut the rock, pierced it, and hewed it until they made it into houses, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And you carve from the mountains houses, skillfully﴾. The poet said:

*Surely everything except God is vain, and every bliss is inevitably passing.*

The fourth: because he had a tall structure and playgrounds upon stakes and ropes, under which games were played for him. This was said by Qatada.

It is also possible (a fifth): that he was "master of the stakes" because of the abundance of palm trees and trees, since they are like stakes in the earth.

One: "qist 'adhab" (a portion of punishment) like the punishment by the whip. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

Two: "khilt 'adhab" (a mixture of punishment), because it is of various kinds. From this is the saying of the poet:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾. Regarding it there are two aspects.

One: "bil-tariq" (on the path).

Two: "bil-intizar" (in waiting), as Tarafa said:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿By the dawn﴾. This is an oath by which God the Exalted swore. Al-fajr is the breaking of morning light from the horizon of the east. There are two dawns. The first of them is elongated like the tail of a wolf (dhanab al-sirhan), appearing as a column of light with no width, then it disappears into a darkness that intervenes. This dawn is called al-fajr al-mubashshir (the heralding dawn) for the morning. Some call it al-kadhib (the false dawn), because it has been "denied" the morning.

It is part of the night and has no effect on prayer or fasting.

As for the second, it is elongated in its light and spreads across the horizon, and it is called al-fajr al-sadiq (the true dawn), because it tells you the truth about the morning. The poet said:

*It drove away the attacking dogs, and increased their fire with the dhu al-subh al-musaddiq, which flutters.*

On it depends the ruling of prayer and fasting, and we have mentioned that earlier.

Regarding God's oath by the dawn there are four sayings. The first: He meant by it the day, and expressed it as "dawn" because it is its beginning. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: al-fajr is the morning that begins the day each day. This was said by Ali, may God be pleased with him.

The third: He meant by it the dawn prayer. This is also related from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: He meant by it the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) specifically. This was said by Mujahid.

Regarding ﴿and ten nights﴾, which is a second oath, there are four sayings. The first: they are the ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah. This was said by Ibn Abbas, and Abu al-Zubayr related from Jabir that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "(By the dawn and ten nights.) He said: The ten of al-Adha."

The second: they are ten from the beginning of Muharram. This was reported by al-Tabari.

The third: they are the last ten nights of Ramadan. This is related from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: they are the ten of Musa, peace be upon him, which God the Exalted completed for him. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿And the even and the odd﴾. This is a third oath, and regarding these two there are nine sayings. The first: they are the prayer, in which there is even and in which there is odd. This was narrated by Imran ibn Husayn from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second: they are the sunset prayer (maghrib), its even part being two rak'as and its odd part the third rak'a. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Abu al-Aliya.

The third: the even is the Day of Sacrifice, and the odd is the Day of Arafah. This was narrated by Ibn al-Zubayr from Jabir from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The fourth: the even is the two days of Mina, the eleventh and twelfth of Dhu al-Hijjah, and the odd is the third day by counting them. This was said by Ibn al-Zubayr.

The fifth: the even is the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah, and the odd is the three days of Mina. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The sixth: the even is creation of every thing, and the odd is Adam and Hawwa. This is because Adam was single, so he was made even by his wife Hawwa, becoming even after being odd. This was narrated by Ibn Nujayh.

The ninth: it is the number, because all of it is even and odd. This was said by al-Hasan.

It is also possible (an eleventh): the even is that which grows, and the odd is that which does not grow.

﴿And the night when it passes﴾. This is a fourth oath, and regarding it there are three aspects.

The first: it is the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr), because mercy spreads in it and it is singled out for increased reward.

The second: it is specifically the night of Muzdalifah, because people gather in it for obedience to God. Muhammad ibn Ka'b was asked about God's saying ﴿and the night when it passes﴾, and he said: "Travel by night, O traveler, and do not spend the night except at Jam'," meaning Muzdalifah.

The third: He meant the generality of the whole night.

Regarding His saying ﴿when it passes﴾ there are three aspects.

The first: when it grows dark. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: when it moves on, because the night moves with the movement of the sun and the celestial sphere, so it shifts from horizon to horizon. From this is the saying of people: "The night came and the day departed."

The third: when its people travel through it, because al-sara is travel by night.

﴿Is there in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾ Regarding "dhu hijr" there are five sayings among the commentators. The first: for one who has intellect (dhu 'aql). This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: for one who has forbearance (dhu hilm). This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: for one who has religion (dhu din). This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The fourth: for one who has a veil/restraint (dhu sitr). This was said by Abu Malik.

The fifth: for one who has knowledge (dhu 'ilm). This was said by Abu Raja'.

Al-hijr means prevention, and from it the name al-hajar (stone) is derived, because of its refusal through its hardness. For this reason the chamber (al-hujra) was so named, because what is in it is prevented by it. From it also comes hajr al-mawla 'alayhi (the guardian's restraint over a ward), because of what it entails of preventing him from disposal. So it is permissible to take its meaning as any one of these interpretations, since each includes prevention.

Muqatil said: "Hal" here is in the place of "inna," and the sense of the statement is: "Indeed there is in that an oath for one of understanding."

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with 'Ad, Iram?﴾ Regarding "Iram" there are seven sayings. The first: that Iram is the land. This was said by Qatada.

The second: Damascus. This was said by Ikrima.

The third: Alexandria. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The fourth: that Iram is a nation among the nations. This was said by Mujahid, and the poet said:

*As Iram mocked him, and they became like the dreams of sleepers.*

The fifth: that it is the name of a tribe from 'Ad. This was said by Qatada.

The sixth: that Iram is the name of the grandfather of 'Ad. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq, and he related from him that it was his father, and that he was 'Ad ibn Iram ibn 'Awad ibn Sam ibn Nuh.

The seventh: that the meaning of Iram is "the ancient," related by Ibn Abi Najih.

The eighth: that it is destruction, as one says: "The sons of so-and-so were destroyed (urima)," meaning they perished. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The ninth: that God the Exalted crushed them with a crushing, making them decayed (rameem), and for this reason He named them. This was said by al-Suddi.

﴿Of the pillars (dhat al-'imad)﴾. Regarding it there are four sayings. The first: "dhat al-tul" (of stature). Ibn Abbas said: it is derived from the saying of people, "a man who is 'mu'ammad'," if he is tall. Qatada claimed that the height of one man among them was twelve cubits.

The second: "dhat al-'imad" because they were people of tents and pillars, moving about seeking rain. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: "dhat al-quwwa wa al-shidda" (of strength and vigor), derived from the strength of pillars. This was said by al-Dahhak. Thawr ibn Yazid related that he said: "I am Shaddad ibn 'Ad, and I am the one who raised the pillars, and I am the one who strengthened with my arm the belly of the blackness. I am the one who buried a treasure at seven cubits that none will bring out except the nation of Muhammad."

The fourth: "dhat al-'imad" meaning the one established with pillars. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿The likes of which were not created in the lands﴾. Regarding it there are two aspects.

One: "the likes of their city, of the pillars, were not created in the lands." This was said by Ikrima.

Two: "the likes of the people of 'Ad were not created in the lands," due to their height and their strength. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿And Thamud, who carved the rock in the valley﴾. Regarding it there are two aspects.

One: meaning they cut the rock, pierced it, and hewed it until they made it into houses, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And you carve from the mountains houses, skillfully﴾. The poet said:

*Surely everything except God is vain, and every bliss is inevitably passing.*

Another said:

*They struck in every hard rock a hewn pillar, with hands of mighty strength from strong forearms.*

Two: its meaning is that they went around to take the rock in the valley, as the poet said:

*Never have I seen a young she-camel before her who carried sixty wasq (loads) and traversed a land with it.*

As for "al-wad" (the valley), Muhammad ibn Ishaq claimed that it is Wadi al-Qura. Abu al-Ashhab related from Abu Nadra who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ), during the expedition to Tabuk, passed by the valley of Thamud, while he was on a reddish-white horse, and he said: 'Hasten your journey, for you are in a cursed valley.'"

﴿And Pharaoh, master of the stakes﴾. Regarding it there are four sayings. The first: that "al-awtad" (the stakes) are the troops, and therefore he was called "master of the stakes" because of the multitude of his troops. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: because he used to torture people with stakes, fastening them to their hands. This was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid. Al-Kalbi said: "With this same thing Pharaoh tortured his wife Asiya bint Muzahim when she believed, until she died."

The third: that "al-awtad" is the building, and he was called "master of the stakes" because of the abundance of his construction. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: because he had a tall structure and playgrounds upon stakes and ropes, under which games were played for him. This was said by Qatada.

It is also possible (a fifth): that he was "master of the stakes" because of the abundance of palm trees and trees, since they are like stakes in the earth.

﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. Regarding it there are four aspects.

One: "qist 'adhab" (a portion of punishment) like the punishment by the whip. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

Two: "khilt 'adhab" (a mixture of punishment), because it is of various kinds. From this is the saying of the poet:

*O Harith, if our blood were poured out, it would be separated until no blood touches blood.*

Three: that it is a pain of the punishment. This was said by al-Suddi.

Four: that every thing with which God punished is a scourge of punishment. This was said by Qatada.

Qatada also said: "The scourge of punishment was drowning."

﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾. Regarding it there are two aspects.

One: "bil-tariq" (on the path).

Two: "bil-intizar" (in waiting), as Tarafa said:

*O blamer, indeed ignorance is among the pleasures of the young man, and indeed death is a lying-in-wait for men.*

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 89, verses 15–20:

﴿And you devour the heritage, devouring greedily.﴾ Al-turath means al-mirath (inheritance). The word *lamman* (لَمًّا) in His saying has four interpretations:

First: it means intensely, as said by al-Suddi.

Second: it means collectively, from their saying *lamamtu al-ta'am lamman*, when I ate the food all at once (jam'an). This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: its meaning is that he devours recklessly (*safaha safan*), as said by Mujahid.

Fourth: when a person consumes his own property, he then swoops down upon the property of others and devours it, without reflecting on what he eats, whether it is impure or pure. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

It may also be understood as a fifth: that he swoops upon what has been forbidden to him and what he has been prevented from.

﴿And you love wealth with abundant love.﴾ On this there are two interpretations:

One: it means much, abundant. This was said by Ibn Abbas. *Al-jamm* is the abundant. The poet said:

*If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive abundantly,*
*and what servant of Yours has not committed wrong (alamma)?*

Second: excessively, you gather its lawful with its unlawful. This was said by al-Hasan.

It may also be understood as a third: that he loves wealth with a love of hoarding it and keeping it in reserve (*ijmam*), not spending it, so he benefits from it neither in religion nor in worldly life. This is the worst condition of the wealthy person.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 89, verses 21–30:**

﴿On that Day, man will remember, but how will remembrance benefit him?﴾ There are two interpretations of this:

The first: he will repent, but how can he repent? Repentance on the Day of Resurrection does not benefit. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: he will remember what he did in his worldly life and what he sent forward for his afterlife. But how will he have remembrance in the Hereafter? Remembrance benefits only in this world. This was said by Ibn Shajarah.

﴿He will say: "Oh, would that I had sent forth for my life!"﴾ There are two meanings for this:

The first: "I had sent forth from my worldly life for my life in the Hereafter." This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: "I had sent forth from my life for my return in the Hereafter." This was mentioned by Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿So on that Day, none will punish as He punishes, and none will bind as He binds.﴾ Al-Kisa'i recited "lā yuʿadhdhibu" and "lā yūthiqu" with a fatha on the dhal and the thaʾ. Its interpretation according to his recitation is: "None will punish the punishment of the disbeliever who says, 'Oh, would that I had sent forth for my life!'" The rest of the readers recited with a kasra on the dhal and the thaʾ. Its interpretation is that none will punish with the punishment of God except one whom God has forgiven. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan. Thus its interpretation according to the first recitation is understood as referring to the Hereafter, and according to the second recitation as referring to this world.

﴿O soul at rest﴾ There are seven interpretations of this:

The first: it means the believing soul. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: the one that answers (the call). This was said by Mujahid.

The third: the one that believes in what God has promised. This was said by Qatadah.

The fourth: the secure one. This is in the reading (ḥarf) of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "O soul that is secure and at rest."

The fifth: the content one. This was said by Muqatil.

The sixth: what some of the people of spiritual insights (aṣḥāb al-khawāṭir) said: the one at rest in this world. "Return to your Lord" means leave it behind.

The seventh: what al-Hasan said, that when God the Exalted wishes to take the soul of His believing servant, the soul becomes at rest in God, the Mighty and Majestic, and God becomes at rest with it.

﴿Return to your Lord﴾ There are two meanings for this:

The first: to your body at the resurrection on the Day of Judgment. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: to your Lord at death in this world. This was said by Abu Salih.

It may also admit a third interpretation: to the reward of your Lord in the Hereafter.

﴿well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ There are two meanings for this:

The first: she is pleased with God, and He is pleased with her. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: she is pleased with the reward of God, and He is pleased with her deeds. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿Enter among My servants﴾ There are three meanings for this:

The first: "among My servant," and this is in the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "Enter among My servant."

The second: "in My obedience." This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: its meaning is "Enter with My servants." This was said by al-Suddi.

﴿and enter My Paradise﴾ There are two sayings about this:

The first: "into My mercy." This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: the Paradise which is the abode of eternity and the dwelling of the righteous. This is the saying of the majority.

Usamah ibn Zayd said: the soul at rest was given the good news of Paradise at death, at the resurrection, and in Paradise.

There is disagreement about who this verse was revealed concerning, and there are four sayings. The first: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr. Ibn ʿAbbas narrated that it was revealed while Abu Bakr was sitting, and he said: "O Messenger of God, how beautiful this is!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, it will be said to you this."

The second: it was revealed concerning Uthman when he endowed the well of Rumah. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: it was revealed concerning Hamzah. This was said by Buraydah al-Aslami.

The fourth: it is general to all believers. This was narrated by Ikrimah and al-Farra'.

The second: the one that answers (the call). This was said by Mujahid.

The third: the one that believes in what God has promised. This was said by Qatadah.

The fourth: the secure one. This is in the reading (ḥarf) of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "O soul that is secure and at rest."

The fifth: the content one. This was said by Muqatil.

The sixth: what some of the people of spiritual insights (aṣḥāb al-khawāṭir) said: the one at rest in this world. "Return to your Lord" means leave it behind.

The first: to your body at the resurrection on the Day of Judgment. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

It may also admit a third interpretation: to the reward of your Lord in the Hereafter.

The first: she is pleased with God, and He is pleased with her. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: its meaning is "Enter with My servants." This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: the Paradise which is the abode of eternity and the dwelling of the righteous. This is the saying of the majority.

The second: it was revealed concerning Uthman when he endowed the well of Rumah. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: it was revealed concerning Hamzah. This was said by Buraydah al-Aslami.

The fourth: it is general to all believers. This was narrated by Ikrimah and al-Farra'.
